title: Would this cooking system be fun to explore, or too much work in a long running strategy game?
author: thecrownforge
selftext:
I'm working on a cooking path for Crownforge, a fantasy city builder. It's still a design I am working on. I want someone who enjoys crafting to have a lot to discover, while a player who just wants to build their city can make or buy useful food without treating it like a daily job.

  


A dish uses a food type, a main ingredient, a side ingredient, a spice and an optional accent. There is a short timing step when you cook it, which changes the quality. The same ingredient combination has the same base result for everyone, so players can learn recipes and share them. Food can go to a tavern menu, become a short feast for PvE(buffs), or be served to visiting heroes who have favourite dishes(get better relation or  easier recruitment).



The ingredient pool is fairly big(or small ): 27 new food ingredients and 10 shared with another craft. Some come from farms and fishing, others from hunts, caravans and later activities. Early food would use common ingredients(T1,T2), and a known recipe could be picked with one tap. If you miss the timing step, you still get an ordinary dish. Would gathering across several activities make this interesting, or just annoying? Is the bigger problem the number of ingredients, remembering combinations, or finding the materials in the first place?



Cooking would grow from T1 to T5, with cook ranks and a specialty for players who want to go deeper into this craft. Ff the useful bonus from food is already capped, would rare T4 and T5 ingredients still feel worth chasing? (it will add another 30% more value than T3)  What would make the later tiers rewarding without making everyone grind cooking?



I'm also thinking about trade. Common ingredients and ready dishes could be sold. For rarer food, a customer could bring their own materials and pay a cook to make the dish. Then there's recipe credit. Should the name on a recipe go to the person who found the combination first, or the first person who cooked a perfect version? Should that name stay forever, or should the first cook stay in a history book while each season can have its own featured cook? If a dish is made on commission, how would you credit the customer and the cook fairly? This would be recognition, not a permanent power bonus.



And one wider question: which game had the best crafting system you've played, and what exactly made it work for you? I'm especially interested in systems where finding materials, learning recipes and trading with other players all felt good together.

Thanks in advance for feedback.  
Andrzej

comments.author: HitMePat
comments.body: Maybe.  Try actually making it so you can show us something besides an image of a cartoon woman in a kitchen.  No one's going to have useful feedback for you based on what essentially boils down to "Would it be fun to gather ingredients, learn recipes, and make dishes?"

replies.author: thecrownforge
replies.body: Fair enough. I will publish an early alpha tomorrow and wanted to get some feedback to have some fixes added to it. What game had the best crafting system in your oppinion?

comments.author: JTxt
comments.body:
Perhaps try it, even as an html javascript ui game with no art to see if it's fun.

It's easy to prototype it using that text.  

Free tip: I like to use voice mode on my phone while I go for a walk to explore/research options, have it grill me on the design, what I want... then have it make a complete spec document.  Then in a new conversation/claude-code, build it.

replies.author: thecrownforge
replies.body: I try to stay less addicted to LLMs and have not used mobile version. Though I will soon go to sleep and just before that I will write a prompt: I will be back in 7 hours". make sure all the prototypes are ready in the morning . Use Astra High to verify the quality before you show me the results" ;)

comments.author: JWalter89
comments.body: AI is really great at making small scale prototypes. You should build a prototype and host it somewhere for people to playtest, and that would give you mich more actionable feedback instead of a long-winded reddit post.

replies.author: thecrownforge
replies.body: I am doing it right now. I will publish an early version tomorrow
